facts.capital: Santa Fe (founded in 1610, the oldest state capital in the U.S.)
facts.statehood_note: New Mexico was a U.S. territory from 1850 until it became the 47th state in 1912.
facts.motto: Crescit eundo (Latin for "It grows as it goes")
borders: Utah (touches only at the Four Corners)
Mexico (the states of Chihuahua and Sonora)
facts.name_origin: The Spanish named the region Nuevo México after the Kingdom of Mexico. The word "Mexico" comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Mexica (Aztec) people, and first meant their homeland in the Valley of Mexico.

government.chambers: New Mexico Senate (42 members) and New Mexico House of Representatives (70 members)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; a governor may not serve more than two terms in a row, but may run again after sitting out a full term). The Lieutenant Governor presides over the Senate.
government.courts: New Mexico Supreme Court (5 justices) is the highest court; below it are the Court of Appeals (10 judges who hear cases in panels of three), district courts in 13 judicial districts, and magistrate, probate, and municipal courts.
government.local: 33 counties; towns may call themselves a village, town, or city. New Mexico's 23 tribal nations are sovereign nations with their own governments.
government.constitution: Drafted at a convention in 1910 and approved by voters on January 21, 1911; it took effect with statehood in 1912. It forbids discrimination based on a person's inability to speak, read, or write English or Spanish, and it reaffirms the rights of Spanish-speaking New Mexicans under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
government.kid_line: "All persons are born equally free, and have certain natural, inherent and inalienable rights" (New Mexico Constitution, Article II, Section 4)

long_ago.about: Hunter-gatherers of the Clovis culture hunted big game on New Mexico's Eastern Plains roughly 11,000 to 9200 BCE. Human footprints found in New Mexico in 2017 suggest people may have been here even earlier.
From about 300 BCE to 1150 CE, Mogollon peoples lived in west-central and southwestern New Mexico. They farmed, made pottery, and lived in villages of pit houses.

From about 850 to 1150, Chaco Canyon was a major center of Ancestral Puebloan culture with great houses like Pueblo Bonito, and a hub of trade. Their descendants are the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico and the Hopi of Arizona.
Taos Pueblo, a terraced, many-story adobe town in northern New Mexico, dates to the late 1200s and early 1300s and has been lived in ever since.

The Navajo (Diné) and Apache arrived in New Mexico by the late 1400s (some experts say earlier). Navajo settlements appear in Chaco Canyon by the 1600s, and Pueblo people sometimes took refuge with the Navajo after 1680.

today.about: The Diné people's sovereign nation, one of New Mexico's 23 tribes.

Acoma, Cochiti, Isleta, Jemez, Laguna, Nambe, Ohkay Owingeh, Picuris, Pojoaque, San Felipe, San Ildefonso, Sandia, Santa Ana, Santa Clara, Santo Domingo, Taos, Tesuque, Zia, and Zuni are each sovereign nations with their own governments.
One of the three Apache tribes the state counts among its 23 tribes.
An Apache nation; Mescalero people were also forced to Bosque Redondo in the 1860s.
An Apache nation based in Oklahoma that New Mexico's Indian Affairs Department counts among the state's 23 tribes.

first_peoples.today_note: New Mexico's Indian Affairs Department says there are 23 tribes in New Mexico: 19 Pueblos, the Navajo Nation, and three Apache tribes. Each is a sovereign nation with its own government, lifeways, traditions, and culture.
sites: Chaco Culture National Historical Park (Ancestral Puebloan great houses, 850 to 1150)
Taos Pueblo (lived in continuously for centuries; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992)
Bandelier National Monument (Ancestral Pueblo rooms carved into soft volcanic tuff)
Statue of Po'pay in the U.S. Capitol's National Statuary Hall (given by New Mexico in 2005)

history.event: Clovis hunter-gatherers hunt big game on the Eastern Plains; people have lived in New Mexico for at least 11,000 years.
Chaco Canyon is a major center of Ancestral Puebloan culture and trade; people later move to new homes, becoming today's Pueblo peoples and the Hopi.
Spanish explorer Francisco Vázquez de Coronado arrives in Pueblo lands.
Juan de Oñate begins Spanish colonization of New Mexico; in 1599 his soldiers carry out the Ácoma Massacre against the people of Acoma Pueblo.
Pedro de Peralta founds Santa Fe as the Spanish capital.
The Pueblo Revolt, led by Po'pay, begins on August 10 and forces the Spanish to leave; it is called the first successful revolution against European rule in the Americas.
Diego de Vargas leads the return of Spanish rule. Under Spain, raids took Apache and Navajo people as captives who were enslaved, causing long-lasting conflict.
Mexico wins independence from Spain, and New Mexico becomes part of Mexico; trade with the United States opens.
During the U.S.-Mexican War, U.S. troops take New Mexico; in 1847 the Taos Revolt against U.S. rule is put down, and the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo gives the land to the United States.
Congress creates the New Mexico Territory as part of the Compromise of 1850.
Civil War: at the Battle of Glorieta Pass (March 26 and 28), Union troops burn the Confederate supply train, and the Confederates leave New Mexico; some call it the "Gettysburg of the West."

On the Long Walk, the U.S. Army forces up to 10,000 Navajo (Diné) and about 500 Mescalero Apache to Bosque Redondo near Fort Sumner, where many die. The Navajo Treaty, signed at Fort Sumner on June 1, 1868, lets the Navajo return to their homeland.
Congress passes the Peonage Act to end the system of debt servitude (peonage) that had existed in New Mexico.

trailblazers.name: Po'pay
trailblazers.group: Pueblo leader (San Juan Pueblo, today Ohkay Owingeh)
trailblazers.text: Po'pay organized the Pueblo Revolt, which began on August 10, 1680, and drove Spanish colonizers out of New Mexico. In 2005 New Mexico gave a statue of him by Pueblo sculptor Cliff Fragua to the U.S. Capitol; the knotted cord in his left hand shows how the start of the revolt was timed.

trailblazers.name: Cathay Williams
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery in Missouri, Cathay Williams enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1866 as "William Cathay," the only known woman to serve as a Buffalo Soldier. Her company served at Fort Union, Fort Cummings, and Fort Bayard in New Mexico Territory until her discharge in 1868.

trailblazers.name: Nina Otero-Warren
trailblazers.text: Born near Los Lunas, Nina Otero-Warren led New Mexico's branch of the Congressional Union in the fight for women's right to vote and insisted that suffrage writings be printed in both English and Spanish. She was Santa Fe County's superintendent of schools from 1918 to 1929 and ran for Congress in 1921.

trailblazers.name: Maria Martinez
trailblazers.text: Maria Martinez learned pottery from her aunt and grandmother at San Ildefonso Pueblo. With her husband Julian Martinez, she revived an old way of making shiny all-black pottery that became famous by the mid-1920s and is now seen as fine art.

trailblazers.name: Dennis Chávez
trailblazers.text: Born in Los Chávez, New Mexico, Dennis Chávez served in the U.S. House and then in the U.S. Senate from 1935 until his death in 1962, the first Hispanic Democrat elected to the Senate. In 1944 he introduced a bill to create a Fair Employment Practices Commission to fight job discrimination.

trailblazers.name: Chester Nez
trailblazers.text: Born in Chi Chil Tah, New Mexico, Chester Nez was one of the original 29 Navajo Code Talkers who served in the U.S. Marine Corps in World War II. He received the Congressional Gold Medal in 2001 and was the last of the original 29.

landforms: Sangre de Cristo Mountains, with Wheeler Peak (13,161 feet), the highest point
Great Plains, including the Llano Estacado
White Sands gypsum dunefield in the Tularosa Basin
waters: Red Bluff Reservoir (lowest point, about 2,840 feet)
geography.regions: New Mexico, the 5th-largest state, includes high mountains (the Sangre de Cristo range), the Great Plains in the east, the Colorado Plateau in the northwest, and the Chihuahuan Desert in the south.

ecosystems.name: White Sands gypsum dunes
ecosystems.about: The world's largest gypsum dunefield covers over 275 square miles. White-colored animals that blend in with the sand are found here, including at least one from every class of vertebrate in North America.

ecosystems.name: Caves of Carlsbad Caverns
ecosystems.about: About 120 caves are known in Carlsbad Caverns National Park, and its Big Room covers 8.2 acres. Carlsbad Cavern holds a colony of about 400,000 Brazilian free-tailed bats.

science.weather: Mostly dry (semi-arid to arid), averaging about 13.7 inches of precipitation a year, with cold alpine weather in the high mountains. Spring is wildfire season; summer monsoon rains usually begin around late June or early July and can cause flash floods, especially on burned land. Temperatures have ranged from 122°F (1994, near Loving) to -50°F (1951, at Gavilan).
science.resources: Mining and oil and gas (boosted by a big oil find near Hobbs in 1928), plus aerospace, film, and science: White Sands Missile Range, Kirtland Air Force Base, Sandia National Laboratories, and Los Alamos National Laboratory are here.
science.highlight: White Sands National Park: the water, rocks, and climate of the Tularosa Basin keep a "gypsum cycle" going that built the largest gypsum dunefield on Earth, over 275 square miles of white sand.

g3_ss.title: New Mexico's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Locate Santa Fe (the oldest state capital) and Albuquerque, learn the 42-member Senate and 70-member House, the governor's job, the 33 counties, and that 23 tribal nations have their own governments; read Article II, Section 4.

g3_ss.title: New Mexico's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Pueblo peoples, the Navajo (Diné), and the Apache nations; visit Taos Pueblo and Chaco Canyon in photos and learn that these nations still live and govern in New Mexico today.

g3_ss.title: New Mexico Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Short biographies of Po'pay, Maria Martinez, Nina Otero-Warren, and Chester Nez, with a 'What did they change?' card for each.

g45_ss.title: New Mexico's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: From Clovis hunters and Mogollon pit-house villages to Chaco Canyon's great houses and the arrival of the Navajo and Apache; trace Chaco's descendants to today's Pueblos and the Hopi.

g45_ss.title: Spanish and Mexican New Mexico
g45_ss.plan: Coronado (1540), Oñate and the Ácoma Massacre (1598 to 1599), Santa Fe (1610), the Pueblo Revolt led by Po'pay (1680), the captive trade and enslavement of Native people, and Mexican rule after 1821.

g45_ss.title: New Mexico 1846 to 1877
g45_ss.plan: U.S. conquest and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the 1847 Taos Revolt, the 1850 territory, Glorieta Pass (1862), Cathay Williams and the Buffalo Soldiers, the Long Walk and the 1868 Navajo Treaty, and the 1867 Peonage Act.

g3_sci.title: White Sands
g3_sci.plan: What gypsum is, how wind builds dunes, and how white-colored animals blend in to stay safe.

g3_sci.title: Bats of Carlsbad Caverns
g3_sci.plan: Meet the Brazilian free-tailed bats (about 400,000 in one colony), how bats use caves, and why they matter.

g3_sci.title: Desert Weather: Monsoon and Fire
g3_sci.plan: Track a dry spring (wildfire season) and the summer monsoon rains; make a safety poster about flash floods.

g45_sci.title: Caves and Underground Rock
g45_sci.plan: Explore Carlsbad Caverns (120 known caves, the 8.2-acre Big Room) and how water and rock shape caves and cave formations.

g45_sci.title: Volcanic Rock and Ancient Homes
g45_sci.plan: Investigate tuff, a soft rock made from volcanic ash flows, and how Ancestral Pueblo people carved rooms and blocks from it at Bandelier.

g45_sci.title: Life in a Dry Land
g45_sci.plan: Compare desert, plains, and mountain habitats; graph New Mexico's 13.7-inch average yearly precipitation against your own state's.
